summary: Lists common IANA allocations for mobile ad hoc network protocols. The needed well-known numbers are a UDP port number, an IP protocol number, and a link-local multicast group address, which many such protocols can share.

plainLanguage.summary: Different wireless network programs all need the same few special numbers, like a shared mailbox address. This note picks them once so every program can use them.

subtitle: Well-known numbers for wireless mesh routing protocols to share.

tldr.problem: Mobile ad hoc network (MANET) routing protocols each need a UDP port, an IP protocol number, and a multicast address. Assigning separate numbers to each protocol wastes scarce resources.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5498 allocates a single set of shared well-known numbers that all MANET protocols conforming to a common format can use together.
tldr.outcome: Interoperable MANET routing protocols can be built on a standard set of port and protocol allocations, and experimentation is simpler when multiple protocols share the same numbers.

today: RFC 5498 is a standards-track specification and is still current. MANET protocols that implement the common format defined in RFC 5444 use these allocations.

sections.title: Sharing Numbers for Ad Hoc Networks
sections.content:
Mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) are wireless networks where devices forward traffic for each other without a central authority. Many different routing protocols exist for MANETs, and they all need the same handful of well-known identifiers to operate.

RFC 5498 defines a shared set of numbers that conforming MANET protocols can use, avoiding duplication. All protocols using these numbers must conform to RFC 5444, which provides a common message format.
sections.plainLanguage: Wireless networks with many independent devices need special numbers so the devices know how to talk to each other.

sections.title: The Well-Known Numbers
sections.content:
Three allocations are specified. First, MANET routers use UDP port 269 to send and receive routing protocol packets. Second, they use IP protocol number 138 for the same purpose. Third, IPv4 routers use the link-local multicast address 224.0.0.109 and IPv6 routers use FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:6D to reach all MANET routers on the local link.

These numbers are assigned to applications named manet in the IANA registries. The multicast address is identified as LL-MANET-Routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Port 269, protocol number 138, and multicast addresses 224.0.0.109 (IPv4) or FF02::6D (IPv6) are the reserved numbers for mesh routing.

sections.title: RFC 5444 Requirement
sections.content:
Any protocol using these allocations must conform to RFC 5444, the Generalized MANET Packet/Message Format. This requirement ensures that when multiple MANET protocols share the same port and protocol number, they can coexist on the same network without colliding.

RFC 5444 provides a common header format that allows routers to parse and dispatch messages from different protocols even when they arrive on the same port.
sections.plainLanguage: All protocols that share these numbers must follow the same message format so they do not confuse each other.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content: RFC 5498 itself defines only the allocations, not the protocols. Each MANET protocol using these numbers may have its own security issues, but those issues are independent of the allocation. However, when multiple protocols share the same port, the specification of each protocol must address how security policies interact.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing numbers does not create new problems, but each protocol must still be secure on its own.

references.text: Clausen, T., Dearlove, C., Dean, J., and C. Adjih, "Generalized Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) Packet/Message Format", RFC 5444, February 2009.
Hinden, R. and S. Deering, "IP Version 6 Addressing Architecture", RFC 4291, February 2006.
